youtube.aciklama:
Tinnitus is a subjective perception, so how are its pitch, loudness and maskability measured? In this lesson we cover pitch matching and octave confusion, why loudness matches come out at a low sensation level, the minimum masking level (MML), residual inhibition, and the limitations of these psychoacoustic measures.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Tyler, Tinnitus Handbook; Henry et al., Computer-automated tinnitus assessment: noise-band matching, maskability, and residual inhibition, J Am Acad Audiol (2013); Vernon and Meikle, Tinnitus: clinical measurement, Otolaryngologic Clinics of North America (2003); NICE, Tinnitus: assessment and management (NG155, 2020); Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn how we match the pitch and loudness of tinnitus with external sounds.
We will also cover the minimum masking level, residual inhibition, and what these measures do and do not show.
Tinnitus is a subjective perception; there is no signal in the ear or brain that we can measure directly.
Psychoacoustic measures let the person describe their tinnitus by comparing it with sounds presented from outside.
The most widely used are pitch matching, loudness matching, the minimum masking level and residual inhibition.
These measures make the person feel their tinnitus is taken seriously and give counseling a concrete starting point.
They can also guide the planning of sound therapy or device settings.
But it is important to know from the start that these measures do not show how much the tinnitus bothers the person.
Psychoacoustic measures are done after a complete audiological assessment.
First the history is taken, and the impact of tinnitus on life is recorded with a scale.
Then pure tone audiometry is done; if possible, frequencies above 8000 hertz are also tested.
A loudness match cannot be read without the thresholds, because the result is expressed relative to the threshold at that frequency.
Next come pitch and loudness matching, and finally the minimum masking level and residual inhibition.
In one-sided tinnitus, the matching sound usually goes to the opposite ear, so the external sound does not affect the tinnitus itself.
Before matching, the person is asked to describe their tinnitus in their own words.
Tonal tinnitus is like a whistle or ringing at a single pitch.
Noise-like tinnitus is described as hissing, buzzing or a sound like wind.
Some people hear several sounds at once; in that case, the most bothersome one is usually matched.
The description decides whether a tone or narrowband noise will be used for matching.
Pitch matching means finding the frequency of the sound that most resembles the tinnitus.
In a common method, two tones are played one after the other, and the person is asked which one sounds more like their tinnitus.
The frequency range is narrowed step by step based on the chosen tone; this is called the two-alternative forced-choice method.
The tones are presented at a level the person hears comfortably, close to the loudness of the tinnitus.
A common error is octave confusion: the person may choose a pitch one octave below or above the true pitch.
So the frequency found is checked by also playing the octave above and the octave below.
For noise-like tinnitus, matching is done with narrowband noise instead of a tone.
The level used for matching is also noted, because the perceived pitch can shift slightly when the level changes.

notlar.metin: Pitch often in the region of loss

cumleler: In this example graph, thresholds start to drop above 2000 hertz.
The person's tinnitus pitch was matched at around 6000 hertz.
In most people, tinnitus pitch falls in the high-frequency region where the hearing loss is.
But pitch matching has low repeatability; results can change markedly even within the same day.
So the measurement is repeated several times, and the result is recorded as a range rather than a single number.
Knowing the pitch can help, for example, in choosing the sound used in sound therapy.

notlar.metin: Start at threshold, small steps up
Result as sensation level: dB SL
Low SL _does not mean_ mild tinnitus

cumleler: Loudness matching compares how loud the tinnitus is perceived to be with an external sound.
At the matched frequency, a tone is raised in small steps from threshold, stopping when the person finds it as loud as their tinnitus.
The result is expressed relative to the threshold at that frequency, as a sensation level in decibels SL.
In this example the threshold is 50 and the match 55 decibels HL, so the tinnitus matches at only 5 decibels SL.
In most people the loudness match comes out only a few decibels above threshold; this is a common finding in the clinic.
One reason is recruitment: at a frequency with hearing loss, even a small increase just above threshold is heard as loud.
So a low SL value does not mean the tinnitus is mild.
There is no strong link between the loudness match and how much the tinnitus bothers the person.
A person with a low loudness match may report severe distress, while someone with a high match may have adapted well.
This is because distress is largely determined by attention and emotional networks.
To measure distress, we use not psychoacoustic tests but the scales we will see in the next lesson.
Still, changes in loudness over time in the same person can add information in follow-up.
Explaining this distinction also matters in counseling, to validate the distress the person experiences.
The minimum masking level, or MML, is the lowest noise level needed to cover the tinnitus completely.
Broadband noise is usually used, and the person's threshold for this noise is found first.
The noise is then raised in small steps, stopping when the person says they can no longer hear their tinnitus.
The result is recorded in decibels SL, relative to the noise threshold.
In most people the MML is low, but in some people the tinnitus cannot be covered even by high-level noise.
The measurement can be done in both ears together or separately; the method used is recorded.
The MML shows how easily the tinnitus is covered by external sounds and can inform the sound therapy plan.
After the MML is found, residual inhibition is usually measured next with the same noise.
Residual inhibition is the temporary reduction or disappearance of tinnitus after the masking noise is stopped.
In a common protocol, the noise is presented at 10 decibels above the MML for 60 seconds.
When the noise stops, the person is asked whether their tinnitus is the same, quieter, or completely gone.
In this example the tinnitus disappears right after the noise and returns to its former level within about two minutes.
The time the tinnitus stays reduced is timed with a stopwatch; if the reduction is partial, this is also noted.
Many people show partial or complete residual inhibition, but the effect usually lasts seconds to minutes.
This measure shows that tinnitus can be suppressed temporarily; it does not mean a lasting treatment.
Psychoacoustic measures have important limitations.
Results can change within a day in the same person, and repeatability is low, especially for pitch.
They do not reliably show the level of tinnitus distress or the response to treatment.

cumleler.yazi: In 2020, the NICE guideline in England did not recommend psychoacoustic tests such as pitch and loudness matching for assessing tinnitus.
cumleler.ses: In twenty twenty, the NICE guideline in England did not recommend psychoacoustic tests such as pitch and loudness matching for assessing tinnitus.

cumleler: The same guideline also does not recommend measuring uncomfortable loudness levels or acoustic reflex testing to investigate tinnitus.
These measures are used in some clinics and in research; when they are done, they are interpreted with their limitations in mind.

cumleler: Psychoacoustic results are recorded on a standard form.
The form includes the test ear, the ear receiving the matching sound, the sound type used, and the frequency.
The loudness match is written both in decibels HL and in decibels SL.
The MML and the duration and type of residual inhibition, partial or complete, are noted.
Only then can repeat measurements made with the same equipment and method be compared.
The date of the measurement and the person's tinnitus status that day are also part of the record.

sahneler.metin: Do not give the patient the loudness match as a single number. Explain that it reflects the auditory system, and that distress will be addressed separately.
cumleler: A clinical tip: when sharing the loudness match with the patient, do not give the number on its own.
A statement like your tinnitus is only 5 decibels may feel as if it belittles the distress the person experiences.
Instead, explain that the measure shows the sound's counterpart in the auditory system, and that the distress will be addressed separately.
Experiencing residual inhibition can be reassuring for many people, as it shows that tinnitus can change.

No distress measure; NICE advises against

cumleler: Pitch matching uses a two-alternative method, and octave confusion must always be checked.
The loudness match often comes out only a few decibels above threshold; one reason is recruitment.
The MML is the lowest noise level that covers the tinnitus; residual inhibition is the temporary reduction after the noise.
These measures do not show tinnitus distress, and the NICE guideline does not recommend them for tinnitus assessment.
